topics.summary: A service moves to another address, but some clients continue sending requests to the old one. A new worker becomes healthy, but it receives every new request because all clients react to the same fresh measurement. A load balancer reports several available workers, yet duplicate execution appears because retries were routed to workers with unrelated receipt databases.

topics.title: 9.1.1 Distinguishing Names, Endpoints, and Instances
topics.summary: A service name represents a logical capability. An endpoint represents a route to one serving location. An instance represents a particular process or deployment generation. These identities can change at different rates. A service name may remain stable while endpoints are replaced; a process may restart at the same address while losing all volatile state.

topics.summary: A client that receives membership updates asynchronously can observe an old update after a newer one. Attach a monotonic revision or another defined ordering token to snapshots. topics.title: 9.2.1 Interpreting Liveness, Readiness, and Degradation
topics.summary: Liveness asks whether a process should continue running under a particular policy. Readiness asks whether it should receive a particular class of work. A degraded service may be alive and able to answer status queries while unable to accept new jobs. One Boolean “healthy” flag often hides these distinctions.

If a liveness probe fails whenever a downstream database is briefly unavailable, an orchestrator may restart every otherwise healthy frontend and make recovery harder. Conversely, a probe that only checks whether a port accepts connections may route traffic to an instance that cannot perform any useful operation.

topics.title: 9.2.2 Choosing a Load-Balancing Objective
topics.summary: Round-robin balances request counts under simple assumptions, not necessarily work. Least-outstanding-request policies approximate load but can be misled by request size and delayed completion observations. Randomized choices reduce some coordination effects but still require a definition of eligible endpoints and resource limits.

blocks.text: Choose the objective before the algorithm. A stateless read service may aim to spread load. A stateful worker system may need affinity so that the same request identity reaches the authority that owns its receipt. A cache service may trade uniform distribution against locality. These are different problems, and one picker cannot satisfy them accidentally.

blocks.text: Client-side measurements are partial and delayed. If every client immediately sends all traffic to the worker with the lowest observed latency, that worker can become overloaded before the measurements catch up. Add damping, bounded concurrency, and randomized selection where appropriate instead of treating a stale metric as an instantaneous global truth.

blocks.text: The companion does not load-balance the integrated job service across independent worker databases. It uses one configured worker endpoint. Later partitioning and replication designs explain what additional authority is required before that scaling change is safe.

topics.summary: A retry is another attempt for the same logical operation, not necessarily permission to choose an unrelated state owner. A stateless read may move freely to another replica under its consistency contract. A stateful mutation may require the same partition or a replicated authority that shares the idempotency record.

reading.title: Engineering case — Recover discovery after a registry generation changes
paragraphs: A client has accepted membership revision 900. The registry is restored from an old backup and begins publishing revision 20. A rule that accepts only larger integers will reject every update until the counter exceeds 900, even if the new snapshot is the intended authority.

The problem is not solved by accepting any smaller revision after a timeout. A delayed old update could then replace current membership. The protocol needs an authority for distinguishing a new registry incarnation from an old message.

One design uses a generation identifier plus an ordered revision within that generation. The generation transition itself must be trusted and explicitly accepted; arbitrary lexical comparison of random identifiers does not establish which authority is newer. Another design uses a persistent monotonic revision service that survives the relevant recovery operations. The correct choice depends on the control plane.

A reconnect protocol can fetch a fresh authoritative snapshot and its watch position together. It then resumes incremental updates from that position. If the watch reports a gap beyond retained history, the client returns to snapshot acquisition instead of pretending the next event reconstructs everything it missed.

Connection pools complicate the transition. Updating the endpoint vector does not immediately remove connections to retired instances. Define whether those connections drain, close immediately, or remain eligible for a bounded class of requests. Mutations with state affinity may need stronger handling than stateless reads.

The companion’s Discovery model uses one monotonically increasing number and rejects nonadvancing updates. It teaches stale-update rejection within one authority domain. It deliberately does not implement registry generation replacement, watches, or connection-pool reconciliation.

Extend the model in a separate exercise with explicit events: accept generation A revision 900, authorize replacement by generation B, accept B revision 1, reject a delayed A revision 901. The important assertion is that an old generation cannot regain authority merely by carrying a numerically larger revision.

This case illustrates a recurring distributed-systems lesson: counters are ordered only within a specified domain. An API must define who owns that domain and what happens when its state is restored, replaced, or lost.
